603.title: Fields white for harvest (John 4:27–42)
603.hook: she leaves her water jar and tells the town; many believe
603.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this passage when they talk about sharing their faith, hearing in the woman's "come, see" a model of inviting someone rather than arguing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living water, and a Samaritan woman at a well at noon. Your line was in spirit and in truth.

Just as Jesus tells her who he is, the disciples come back with lunch. John says they marveled that he was talking with a woman, and nobody dared ask him why. A group of men holding bread, standing awkwardly. The woman doesn't wait for anyone to explain. She walks fast back toward town, and she leaves the one thing she came for sitting by the well. "The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city."

Why mention the jar? It was the whole reason for her trip. Leaving it says she's in a hurry, and maybe that she'll be back. Some readers hear more: she came for ordinary water and found living water, so the old jar can wait. In town, her message is simple, almost funny: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Not a sermon. An invitation, and a question, close to the one Jesus first asked back in chapter one: what seek ye? Meanwhile, the disciples are pushing food at Jesus. Master, eat. He says, "I have meat to eat that ye know not of." Meat, in King James English, just means food. They wonder if someone brought him something. His food, he explains, is to do the will of the one who sent him. Then he points at the fields: "Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest." Some readers picture the townspeople at that moment, streaming across the fields toward the well, maybe in light-colored clothes. The text doesn't say so, but the timing fits. Many Samaritans believe because of her word. Then Jesus stays two days, more believe, and they tell her: "Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves." She brought them; they met him themselves. And they call him the Savior of the world.

Think of something good that happened to you lately, a kindness, a book, a moment that opened something, and picture the face of someone who'd want to hear about it. Then name your water jar, the small thing that usually stops you sharing, being busy or worrying it'll sound strange, and let it sit by the well a while. If you pray, ask for the nerve to say come and see; if not, just rest with the person you pictured.
Harvest. Jesus's words as the Samaritan town comes out to meet him: the harvest isn't months away, it's already here.
Your line: she left her water jar. The errand could wait. Day six hundred three.

604.title: Go, your son lives (John 4:43–54)
604.hook: a royal official believes the word and walks home
604.tomorrow: do you want to be healed?
604.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this story when someone they love is ill and far away, and some churches pray for the sick by name during worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a water jar left by a well, and a town coming out across fields white for harvest. Your line was she left her water jar.

A man with rank, and none of it helps. The King James calls him a nobleman, an official of the king, and his son is at the point of death in Capernaum. He hears Jesus is back in Galilee, at Cana, the village of the wedding, and goes up to find him. Every hour he's gone is an hour he's not at his son's bed. He doesn't make a speech. He begs: "Sir, come down ere my child die." Come down. Come with me. Now.

Jesus's first answer sounds like a sigh, aimed at the whole crowd as much as at him: "Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe." The father doesn't argue. He asks again. And Jesus doesn't come. He says one short sentence: "Go thy way; thy son liveth." No touch, no visit, no proof. Then John writes today's line: "And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way." Think about that walk. He begged Jesus to come, and he's leaving without him, carrying nothing but a sentence. The next day, still on the road, his servants run to meet him. Your son lives. When did he start getting better? "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The very hour Jesus said go. And John says the man believed, and his whole household with him. The word believe appears twice. First he believes the word, enough to start walking. Then, when he sees what happened, he believes in a fuller way: a step on trust, then sight. John counts this as the second sign Jesus did in Galilee, after the water turned to wine, both from Cana. One at a wedding, one by a word spoken from a distance.
screen: `A LONG ROAD WITH ONLY A SENTENCE.`
then, large: `THE MAN BELIEVED THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Think of a word someone has given you that you can't check yet: a friend's I'll be there, a doctor's this will heal, a line from scripture you hold onto. Notice whether part of you wants proof first, then picture taking the first step home anyway, with only the sentence in your pocket. If you pray, hold that word before God; if you don't, rest with it a moment.
Go. Jesus's answer to a desperate father: go thy way, thy son liveth. One word that sends him home on nothing but trust.
Your line: he believed the word. The seeing came later, on the road. Six hundred four days in.

605.title: Do you want to be healed? (John 5:1–9)
605.hook: a man by the pool thirty-eight years; Jesus asks the obvious question
605.carry: do you want to be well?
605.howItsDone: Christians often read this story in services of prayer for healing; some churches anoint the sick with oil, and many simply pray for people by name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a father walked home on nothing but a sentence: go thy way, thy son liveth. Your line was he believed the word.

Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate. A pool ringed by covered walkways, and under them, sick people lying on mats: blind, lame, withered. "Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches." For centuries some readers thought the five porches were invented, a symbol. Then archaeologists dug near the Church of Saint Anne and found two large pools with colonnades: four around the sides and one across the middle. Five. Under one lies a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years.

Jesus learns how long he's been there and asks a question that sounds almost rude: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Of course he does. Doesn't he? But he doesn't say yes. "Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me." People believed the first one in when the water stirred would be healed. Thirty-eight years, and not one friend to carry him the last few feet. His answer is a list of reasons, and underneath it, loneliness. That's why the question isn't rude. After a long time, a life gets built around what's wrong: your days, your friends, your sense of who you are. Being well would change everything, and change is frightening. Jesus doesn't argue, and he doesn't use the pool. "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk." "And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath." That last phrase is a fuse; it goes off tomorrow. One detail for the curious: some older Bibles, including the King James, have a verse about an angel stirring the water. The earliest Greek manuscripts don't include it, so many modern Bibles put it in a footnote. Either way, John's story turns on the question, not the pool.
screen: then, large: `DO YOU WANT TO BE WELL?`

segments.voice: Think of one thing in your life that isn't well, a habit, a hurt, a grudge, and hear the question: do you want to be well? Don't answer quickly; notice if your first answer is a reason, like the man's, and whether part of you is afraid of what would change. If you pray, bring the honest answer to God; if you don't, hold it gently.
Whole. What Jesus asked a man ill for thirty-eight years if he wanted to be, before he answered with reasons and got up and walked.
Your line: do you want to be well? It's a real question, and a kind one. See you tomorrow.

606.title: My Father works (John 5:10–30)
606.hook: healing on the sabbath: my Father is working still, and so am I
606.howItsDone: Christians read this passage as a teaching about Jesus as the Son of God; some also see in it a call to join in God's ongoing work of healing and care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thirty-eight years by a pool, and a question: wilt thou be made whole? Your line was do you want to be well?

A man walks through Jerusalem with his rolled-up mat under his arm. It's the sabbath, the day of rest that Jewish law protects, and some of the religious leaders stop him: it is not lawful to carry your bed today. His answer is wonderfully human: the man who healed me told me to. Who was it? He doesn't know. He never got the name; Jesus had slipped away into the crowd. Later Jesus finds him in the temple, and the question of the sabbath reaches Jesus himself.

Jesus tells him: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee." The man goes and tells the leaders who healed him, and the argument begins. Remember, this is a debate among Jews about what keeping the sabbath means. Jesus answers in one sentence: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work." Hitherto means until now. Genesis says God rested on the seventh day. Yet the world keeps going on the sabbath: babies are born, rain falls, hearts beat. Jewish teachers asked the same question: how can God rest, when the world needs holding up every moment? Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of that time, answered that God never stops making and sustaining the world. Jesus stands inside that thought: if the Father is still at work, the Son works with him. His listeners hear the claim clearly: he is calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Then he describes how it works between them: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do." Like an apprentice at a workbench, watching the master's hands and copying them. In Christian teaching, this passage is a key to who Jesus is: not a rival to God, but the Son doing what the Father does. And in Jesus's words it's a picture of a God who doesn't clock out, still at the work of healing and giving life.
screen: then, large: `MY FATHER WORKETH HITHERTO, AND I WORK.`

segments.voice: Notice what's working in you right now without any effort: your heart beating, your lungs filling, the ground holding you up. Then picture one small good work you could do, a message to someone lonely, a repair you've put off, carrying something for someone. If you pray, ask to see where God is already at work, and join in; if you don't, choose the work anyway.
Hitherto. It means until now, in Jesus's answer when he healed on the sabbath: My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
Your line: god is still working. Even on the day of rest. Day six hundred six, done.

607.title: Search the scriptures (John 5:31–47)
607.hook: you search the scriptures, yet won't come to me
607.howItsDone: Some Christians read a Bible passage every day, and some practice slow, prayerful reading such as lectio divina, listening for God speaking through the text rather than only studying it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mat carried on the sabbath, and Jesus saying: my Father worketh hitherto. Your line was god is still working.

You can know everything about a person and still not know them. You can read every review of a restaurant and never eat there, or study a map of a city for years and never walk its streets. Yesterday's argument in Jerusalem now turns to evidence: who says you are who you say you are? In that world, a claim needed witnesses; the law of Moses said a matter stands on two or three. So Jesus calls his witnesses, one by one, the way a lawyer would. The last one is a book.

First witness: John the Baptist. "He was a burning and a shining light," and people were glad to stand in that light for a while. Second: the works, the healings and signs, the man walking with his mat. Third: the Father himself. Fourth: the scriptures. "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me." There's a puzzle in the Greek. The verb can be a command, search the scriptures, which is how the King James translators took it. Or a plain statement: you search the scriptures. Other translations read it that way. Same letters, both readings possible. Either way, the next line is the point: "And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life." Jesus doesn't tell them to stop searching. His point is about where reading leads. A map points to a city. A letter points to the one who wrote it. In Christian reading, the scriptures are meant to lead to a living person, not just to more knowledge about him. Christians hear this line in different ways. Some hear it about the Old Testament promises Christians see fulfilled in Jesus. Others hear a warning for anyone who studies: it's possible to know the text by heart and miss the one it's about.
screen: then, large: `THEY ARE THEY WHICH TESTIFY OF ME.`

Instead of asking what it means, ask who is speaking, and what they might be like. If you pray, ask to meet the one the words are about; if you don't, notice the difference between reading for facts and listening for a voice.
Witnesses. Jesus calls them one by one to answer who he is: John, his works, the Father, and the scriptures themselves.
Your line: the scriptures point to him. A map is not the city. That's day six hundred seven.

608.title: Twelve baskets left (John 6:1–15)
608.hook: gather the fragments so nothing is lost
608.howItsDone: Some Christians give thanks before meals, as Jesus does here, and some churches run food banks and community meals, gathering surplus food so nothing is wasted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four witnesses, and the last was a book. Your line was the scriptures point to him.

A crowd on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee, about five thousand men, John says. Passover is near, the feast that remembers the night Israel left Egypt. Jesus asks Philip, as a test: where shall we buy bread for all these? Philip does the math and gives up: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." Not even a little each. Then Andrew notices a boy.

Andrew says: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Matthew, Mark and Luke tell this story too, but John is the one who mentions the boy, and that the loaves were barley. A kid's lunch, offered to a crowd. Jesus has everyone sit on the grass. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Everyone eats until full. The Gospels don't describe how it happened, only what people saw: enough. Then the part this day is named for: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." The disciples go around the hillside collecting broken pieces, and fill twelve baskets. A miracle has just happened, and the next thing Jesus cares about is the crumbs. Twelve baskets: one for each disciple doing the gathering, maybe, or a number some readers connect with the twelve tribes of Israel. All four Gospels tell this feeding, and some Christians hear in it the Lord's Supper too: he took bread, gave thanks, and gave it. And the scene ends strangely. The crowd wants to seize Jesus and make him king by force. He slips away alone, up the mountain. He came to feed them, not to be crowned by them.

Picture your kitchen, half a loaf, a few vegetables, last night's rice, and find one thing that might get thrown out that you could use. Then widen it: a half-finished letter, an hour you usually waste, a small skill nobody asks for. If you pray, give thanks for what's already there, the way Jesus gave thanks over a boy's lunch; if you don't, simply notice how much is there.
Fragments. What the disciples gathered after five thousand ate, so that nothing would be lost: twelve baskets of broken pieces.
Your line: let nothing be lost. Even the crumbs count, all twelve baskets of them. Rest well.

609.title: It is I (John 6:16–21)
609.hook: rowing in the dark, they see him and he says: it is I, be not afraid
609.tomorrow: I am the bread of life
609.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this story in times of fear, and "be not afraid" is repeated in prayers, in hymns and at bedsides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy's lunch fed a hillside, and twelve baskets of fragments. Your line was let nothing be lost.

Evening. Jesus is still alone up the mountain, and the disciples don't wait. They go down to the shore, get into the boat, and start rowing across the lake toward Capernaum. "And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them." Then a great wind blows, and the sea rises. They row, and row. And far out on the lake, in the dark, they see something on the water.

"So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs, they see Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing nigh unto the ship: and they were afraid." And he says: "It is I; be not afraid." In English, it is I sounds like any friend calling out in the dark: it's me. In Greek the words are ego eimi, which simply mean I am, the ordinary way to say it's me. Some readers also hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush, I AM. John will use those two words again, and some readers hear both meanings here at once: it's me, your friend, and I AM, out on the water, where in the book of Job it is God who treads upon the waves. Then the comfort: be not afraid. Fear not is said often in the Bible, by angels, by prophets, and by Jesus more than once. John's ending is lovely and strange: "Then they willingly received him into the ship: and immediately the ship was at the land whither they went." No calming of the storm is described. Just him in the boat, and suddenly the shore.
